comparator.name: Artificial Intelligence
comparator.sourceNotes: The controlling 2026–2027 EER establishes the current 180 EC degree structure:60 EC first year, 48 EC compulsory plus 12 EC restricted choices in year 2, and 24 EC restricted choices, 24 EC free electives and a 12 EC thesis in year 3. The current prospective webpages corroborate component weights but describe an indicative next-academic-year overview; they do not establish a guaranteed future entrant schedule. Current formal eligibility controls this reconstruction. Cognitive Science is restricted to B 2 AI students from cohort 2025, so it is omitted. Select the first eligible year 2 options in webpage order that fill 12 EC:Bayesian Networks 3, Cognitive Computational Neuroscience 3, Explainable AI 3, Sustainable AI 3. The first five eligible listed year 3 options fill 24 EC. This neutral choice is independent of UCR fit; no formal named track is inferred. Positive first-year study advice is needed for B 2; B 3 requires all first-year units; the thesis requires at least 120 EC. RADAr English is a mandatory 0 EC diagnostic. The current programme webpage gives 42 EC for first-year positive advice, subject to personal circumstances; the EER generic appendix retains an unfilled range and does not override that specific figure. Free electives at Dutch universities need no Examination Board permission; other institutions require permission and mandatory courses cannot be counted again. Theoretical Modeling 9 EC replaces the older 6 EC course and excludes students who already passed it.

core: Artificial intelligence, intelligent agents and computational models
Programming, algorithms, software and computer systems
Mathematics, logic, probability, statistics and data modelling
Machine learning, neural networks, deep learning and reinforcement learning
Cognition, psychology, neuroscience, perception and learning
Robotics, autonomous systems, computer vision and human-centred design
Ethics, philosophy and societal impact of artificial intelligence
Experimental design, research methods, academic communication and independent research
adjacent: Computational AI and autonomous intelligent systems
Applications of AI in science and society
questions: How can intelligent systems learn, reason, plan and act?
What can computational models reveal about human thought, perception, language and the brain?
How should AI systems be designed and evaluated for people and society?

trace: develops academic, collaborative and reflective skills for responsible interdisciplinary study
Direct research-methods contribution: operationalisation, experimental design, sampling, inference and a group research project support empirical AI and cognitive-science inquiry.
provides Python programming, debugging, discrete-mathematics and computational problem-solving foundations
provides calculus, equations and mathematical problem-solving foundations for AI and modelling
develops data cleaning, manipulation, visualisation and an independent applied data project
examines fairness, bias, privacy, accountability, human agency and the moral status of AI systems
develops logic, discrete structures and mathematical reasoning for computer science and algorithms
covers planning, uncertainty, partial observability and optimisation for intelligent agents
develops search, games, constraint satisfaction and optimisation for rational agents
Direct AI method: reinforcement-learning frameworks and implemented neural-network agents learn through interaction and trial and error.
develops understanding of network architectures, operating systems, concurrency and resource management
provides relational-database, SQL, normalisation and query-processing foundations
develops software design, testing, maintenance and programming across multiple paradigms
develops algorithm design, data structures and experimental performance analysis
extends algorithmic thinking through algebraic algorithms, mathematical modelling and optimisation
introduces regression, classification, resampling, support-vector machines, trees and clustering
develops image processing, feature detection, tracking, object recognition and computer vision
develops neural-network and deep-learning theory and implementation for vision and language applications
develops robotics through kinematics, manipulation, motion planning and collision avoidance
provides matrices, vector spaces, eigenvalues and linear transformations used in computational models
develops numerical algorithms, approximation and computational solutions to mathematical problems
provides probability theory, distributions, estimation, simulation and statistical inference
Direct cognitive foundation: psychological theories, functional brain anatomy, neural communication and behavioural research methods support the target’s cognition/computation relationship.
develops neurobiological foundations and experimental understanding of brains and behaviour
examines neural mechanisms of sensory processing, perception and goal-directed action
examines memory, attention, emotion, consciousness, decision-making and cognitive control

Direct human-language contribution: neurobiological and psychological language production, comprehension, acquisition and impairments; supports cognitive linguistics rather than providing a dedicated computational NLP sequence.

Complementary social-cognition perspective: studies how others influence thoughts, feelings and behaviour; relevant to human interaction with intelligent systems, without claiming an AI-design course.
develops multivariate statistics and experimental analysis for complex human data
Direct evidence-synthesis method: systematic reviews, meta-analysis, effect sizes and R support evaluation of cognitive and behavioural research; this is not a separate primary-research thesis.

Complementary developmental perspective: cognitive, physical, social and emotional development across the lifespan qualifies how human capacities change; it does not teach computational developmental modelling.
examines consciousness, the mind-body problem and the possibility of intelligent or conscious machines
Complementary conceptual inquiry: free will, luck, time and selfhood support critical examination of agency in the target’s philosophical study of intelligence; no AI implementation is claimed.

Direct mathematical-methods contribution: characterises signals and linear time-invariant systems using convolution, Fourier representations/transforms, Laplace and Z transforms; supplies substantial signal-processing content relevant to the target.

alternatives.label: Artificial intelligence, cognition & intelligent systems
alternatives.concept: Programming, mathematical methods and machine learning combine with robotics, reinforcement learning, signal processing and cognitive neuroscience. Human perception, higher cognition and language supply the cognitive-science strand of this broad AI programme.
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum integrates computational AI with substantial cognitive-science and intelligent-systems study, so the label names all three organising elements.
progression: All formal prerequisites precede their dependent courses and assigned terms follow the current enriched workbook. Programming and mathematical foundations come first; introductory data/research/brain study precedes advanced work where feasible. The300level code alone creates no extra prerequisite.

alternatives.label: Computational AI & autonomous systems
alternatives.concept: Programming, algorithms, software, data infrastructure and mathematical modelling organise this computational AI programme. Machine learning, reinforcement learning, robotics and computer vision develop intelligent systems, supported by research methods, AI ethics and an introduction to brain and behaviour.
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum's dense programming, algorithms, mathematics, learning, optimisation and robotics sequence supports a computational and autonomous-systems label.
alternatives.distinctness: Computational AI places materially more weight on databases,networks,software,advanced algorithms,numerical methods and reinforcement learning. It reduces the broad programme’s neurobiology,perception,higher cognition,psycholinguistics and signal-processing strand; this changes the organising curriculum rather than its label.
progression: All formal prerequisites precede their dependent courses and assigned terms follow the current enriched workbook. Programming and mathematical foundations come first; introductory data/research/brain study precedes advanced work where feasible. The300level code alone creates no extra prerequisite.

alternatives.label: Cognitive AI, language & neuroscience
alternatives.concept: Cognitive neuroscience, human language, psychology and philosophy organise this cognitive AI programme. Programming, machine learning, neural networks, computer vision, optimisation and statistics connect the study of mind and brain to computational methods; research training includes experimental design and evidence synthesis.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed programme combines AI methods with a sustained sequence in cognitive science, neuroscience, psychology, language and philosophy.
alternatives.distinctness: The cognitive programme replaces robotics,software,reinforcement learning and much systems infrastructure with social and developmental psychology,philosophy of mind,agency,and evidence synthesis. A sustained neurocognitive/language sequence remains connected to substantial computing and AI methods.
progression: All formal prerequisites precede their dependent courses and assigned terms follow the current enriched workbook. Programming and mathematical foundations come first; introductory data/research/brain study precedes advanced work where feasible. The300level code alone creates no extra prerequisite.

candidates.label: Computational AI and autonomous intelligent systems

selection.assessment: The broad closest match is complemented by two generator-backed and feasible organising directions: computational AI and autonomous intelligent systems; and cognitive AI, language and neuroscience. Each produces material curricular consequences and exceeds the pairwise 30-EC distinctness floor, so the maximum of three UCR alternatives is reached. Application-sector outcomes such as healthcare, transport, finance and education support these directions but do not independently generate additional alternatives.

blocks: Both provide introductory programming and computational problem-solving foundations.
Both develop programming beyond the introductory level; UCR emphasises software engineering and multiple paradigms.
Dedicated programming-language concepts are not reproduced by an advanced algorithms course. Software Development uses C++ and Haskell, but no equivalent language-concepts syllabus is established.
Both address symbolic or knowledge-based intelligent behaviour, planning and reasoning under constraints.
UCR builds AI across several courses but has no single scheduled survey identical to this introductory component.
UCR courses address intelligent systems and social application, but no single course reproduces this restricted elective.
Both develop predictive modelling from data; UCR surveys major machine-learning methods.
Both provide substantial neural-network and deep-learning theory and implementation.
Both directly develop reinforcement-learning theory and algorithms.
Both provide dedicated robotics study; UCR emphasises kinematics, manipulation and motion planning.
Both provide foundational calculus and mathematical methods for later modelling.
Both develop linear-algebra foundations through matrices, vectors and transformations.
Both develop formal reasoning, logic and discrete structures for AI.
Both introduce probability foundations; UCR combines probability with statistical inference.
Both develop statistical modelling and analysis; UCR focuses on multivariate and experimental human-data methods.
Both extend mathematical problem solving; UCR emphasises numerical algorithms rather than a second calculus sequence.
Both provide research design, experiments, sampling and introductory statistical methodology.
UCR Probability & Statistics covers inference and probability, but not a dedicated six-credit Bayesian-statistics sequence.
UCR AI and probability courses provide related tools but no single dedicated Bayesian-networks course.

Both provide broad psychological and cognitive foundations; UCR integrates these with neuroscience and behaviour.
Both provide biological foundations for understanding the brain.
Human psycholinguistics does not reproduce the computational representations,algorithms and modelling methods of dedicated natural-language processing.
UCR combines neurobiology, cognition and computation across courses but has no single dedicated computational-neuroscience component.
UCR offers neuroscience, perception and computing courses but no dedicated brain-computer-interface course.
UCR supports computational and cognitive modelling across courses but not a nine-credit dedicated theoretical-modelling component.
Both critically examine ethical and societal consequences of AI, including responsibility, fairness and human agency.
No scheduled course establishes dedicated human-centred design methods. Psychological insight and AI ethics support the wider programme but do not substitute for this design component.
Both develop personal, academic and professional formation in the first year.
UCR develops academic skills across its curriculum and PPD, but has no separate five-credit AI-specific academic-skills course.
UCR develops research and communication across several courses but not as a dedicated AI design-and-communication component.
UCR includes AI ethics and philosophy of mind but no dedicated philosophy-of-science-for-AI course.
UCR requires first-year PPD but has no separate second-year PPD continuation.
UCR AI Ethics examines fairness and bias, but no single course reproduces this dedicated intersectional-theory elective.
AI Ethics includes clinical and therapeutic contexts, but no scheduled course provides a dedicated AI-ethics-in-healthcare component.
The comparator preserves 24 EC of genuine free choice.
No scheduled course provides a dedicated explainable-AI syllabus.
No scheduled course provides a dedicated sustainable-AI syllabus.

notes.text: Radboud integrates computing, mathematics, statistics, cognitive science, neuroscience, linguistics and philosophy with a required 12 EC thesis. UCR can construct substantial AI programmes with different computational and cognitive emphases. They retain gaps in dedicated Bayesian methods, NLP, human-centred design, brain-computer interfacing and theoretical cognitive modelling. Signal processing is present only in the broad UCR programme. Evidence synthesis and other scheduled research work do not replace Radboud’s separate thesis; optional independent research is additional to the 24-course plan.

audience.programmeDescription: Radboud’s English-taught Artificial Intelligence bachelor studies human cognition and develops intelligent computer systems. Programming, mathematics, statistics, robotics, neuroscience, language and philosophy support a 180 EC degree with restricted electives, free choice and a required thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Three related UCR programmes emphasise broad AI and cognition, computational intelligent systems, or cognitive neuroscience and language. Each contains substantial AI methods but differs from Radboud’s integrated specialist sequence. Human language study is distinct from computational NLP, and the UCR schedules do not replace the separate Radboud thesis.

curriculum.limitation: This pathway uses the current 2026–2027 regulations. Prospective webpages describe an indicative overview that may change; future cohort availability is not guaranteed. Year 2 contains 12 EC restricted choices and year 3 contains 24 EC restricted choices plus 24 EC free electives. The cohort 2025-only Cognitive Science option is excluded. Year 2 requires positive study advice; year 3 requires all first-year units; the thesis requires 120 EC. RADAr English is an additional 0 EC requirement. The programme publishes a 42 EC first-year continuation threshold, subject to personal circumstances.
